rows: Q fever is a zoonotic infection caused by Coxiella burnetii.
Cattle, sheep and goats are important animal reservoirs.
Infection can follow inhalation of contaminated aerosols or dust.
Birth products and manure can contain high concentrations of the organism.
Illness ranges from asymptomatic infection to febrile or organ-specific disease.
Occupational and farm exposures should be considered during assessment.
Prevention includes hygiene, animal-management and exposure controls.
Outbreak investigation uses human, animal and environmental information.
Farm proximity or fever does not establish Q fever.
Conclusions require animal event, exposure route, timing, symptoms, laboratory and epidemiological evidence.
Hantaviruses are zoonotic viruses associated mainly with rodents.
Transmission can occur through inhalation or contact with contaminated rodent material.
Different hantaviruses can cause renal or cardiopulmonary syndromes.
Travel, rodent and occupational histories are important in assessment.
Specialist laboratory testing is available through UKHSA.
Suspected Andes-virus infection requires enhanced infection-control consideration.
Some hantavirus diseases are urgent notifiable conditions.
Contacts and incidents should be managed using current strain-specific guidance.
Rodent contact or fever does not establish hantavirus infection.
Conclusions require virus, geography, exposure, symptoms, laboratory, timing and public-health assessment.
West Nile virus is mainly maintained between birds and mosquitoes.
Humans are usually infected through mosquito bites.
Many infections are asymptomatic or mild.
A small proportion can develop neuroinvasive disease.
Travel and mosquito-exposure history are important.
Suspected encephalitis is a notifiable clinical condition.
Prevention focuses on mosquito-bite avoidance and surveillance.
A mosquito bite or encephalitis does not establish West Nile virus infection.
Conclusions require geography, season, exposure, symptoms, laboratory and surveillance evidence.
Chikungunya is transmitted mainly by infected Aedes mosquitoes.
Fever and severe joint pain are common presenting features.
Symptoms usually begin several days after an infectious bite.
Illness can be confused with dengue and other viral infections.
Joint symptoms can persist after the acute illness.
Travel history is important in assessment.
Prevention focuses on avoiding mosquito bites in risk areas.
Fever and joint pain after travel do not establish chikungunya.
Conclusions require destination, exposure, timing, symptoms, testing and differential-diagnosis evidence.
